Operator: Good day, and welcome to the Global Asset Partners Second Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question and answer session. To ask a question, you will need to register by pressing star, then one on your telephone keypad. To withdraw your question, please press star, then two. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Global Asset Partners' Second Quarter 2024 results. Joining me on today's call are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Emily Carter, Chief Financial Officer; Michael Reynolds, Chief Investment Officer; and David Patel, Head of Distribution.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that some of the statements made today may be forward-looking. Please refer to our SEC filings for a discussion of the risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially.

With that, I'll turn the call over to Johnathan.

Johnathan Hale: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us. I'm pleased to report on our performance for the second quarter of 2024. We achieved solid results this quarter, driven by robust net inflows, favorable market appreciation, and our focus on higher-margin products. Our AUM grew to $585 billion.

Emily Carter: Thank you, Johnathan. From a financial perspective, Global Asset Partners delivered strong results in the second quarter of 2024. Our revenue was $1.8 billion, representing an 11% increase year-over-year. This growth was primarily driven by our core revenue streams, particularly management fees, alongside prudent expense control. Our expenses were $1.11 billion, resulting in net income of $650 million. We continue to manage our expenses prudently, as evidenced by our operating margin trends and compensation discipline.

Let me now turn to our core revenue drivers, starting with management fee revenue and average fee rate trends, which remain the bedrock of our recurring revenue model here at Global Asset Partners. For the second quarter of 2024, management fee revenue came in at $1.25 billion, up 9% year-over-year and 5% quarter-over-quarter. This performance exceeded our internal guidance and reflects a combination of robust net inflows, favorable market appreciation, and disciplined fee management across our $585 billion in assets under management, or AUM, as of quarter-end—up 14% from Q2 2023.

Breaking this down by key drivers, AUM growth was propelled by $18 billion in long-term net inflows during the quarter, bringing year-to-date inflows to $32 billion. This marks our strongest H1 inflow performance since 2021, driven primarily by our institutional channel, which accounted for 65% of inflows. Retail and intermediary flows were solid at $6 billion, bolstered by our enhanced SMA platform, which now serves over 1.2 million high-net-worth clients through partnerships with RIAs like those integrated with Envestnet and Orion Advisor Tech.

Market returns contributed an additional $25 billion to AUM, with our equity strategies capturing the broad rally—particularly in U.S. large-cap growth, where the S&P 500 returned 15% quarter-to-date amid the AI infrastructure buildout led by names like NVIDIA and Broadcom. Our fixed income AUM benefited from the 2% total return in investment-grade credit, as anticipated Fed rate cuts in September supported duration extension.

Shifting to average fee rate trends, our blended fee rate stood at 44.5 basis points for the quarter, down modestly 20 bps year-over-year from 46.5 bps, but stable sequentially. This reflects ongoing industry-wide fee compression, particularly in our beta-oriented equity and core fixed income strategies, where we've seen competitive pressure from low-cost ETF providers like Vanguard's VTI or BlackRock's iShares Core lineup. In response, we've strategically de-emphasized lower-margin index mutual funds, allowing them to organically decline as a percentage of AUM from 28% to 25% over the past year.

However, this compression has been more than offset by mix shift toward higher-fee products. Our alternatives and multi-asset solutions, which carry average fees of 85 bps, now represent 22% of AUM—up from 18% a year ago—driving 150 bps of positive mix impact. Key contributors include private markets expansion: Our private credit fund, GAP Private Credit Opportunities, raised $4.5 billion in commitments this quarter at a 1.25% management fee plus 15% carried interest, mirroring the success of peers like Ares Management. Year-to-date, alts inflows hit $12 billion, fueled by pension plans seeking yield in a higher-for-longer rate environment.

ESG and thematic strategies also played a big role: Our suite of Article 8 and 9 UCITS funds under SFDR grew AUM by 25% YoY to $45 billion, with fees averaging 55 bps. Institutional demand from European clients remains strong, despite regulatory scrutiny, as we leverage our proprietary ESG data analytics powered by our AI-driven risk platform, similar to BlackRock's Aladdin enhancements.

Regionally, the trends vary meaningfully. In the Americas, which comprise 62% of AUM, fee rates held steady at 46 bps, supported by sticky U.S. institutional mandates in equities and our growing 401(k) wrap programs. Europe, at 24% of AUM, saw a slight uptick to 48 bps, driven by PRIIPs-compliant ETFs and MiFID II fee transparency, where we've optimized disclosures to retain €25 billion in AUA. APAC, now 10% of AUM following our acquisition of a Singapore-based boutique last year, delivered the strongest fee lift at 52 bps, with $3 billion in inflows into our China A-shares strategy amid the CSI 300 rebound and RQFII quota expansions.

From a technical standpoint, we've deployed several initiatives to arrest fee erosion. Our fee optimization engine, built on machine learning models akin to those at State Street Global Advisors, analyzes client cohorts to proactively offer tiered fee schedules—resulting in a 5% reduction in fee waivers this quarter. We've also accelerated our ETF conversion program, launching five new active ETFs in Q2 with target fees of 35-45 bps, undercutting mutual fund equivalents while preserving economics through scale. This positions us competitively against ARK Invest's thematic ETFs or Fidelity's ZERO lineup, with early AUM surpassing $2 billion.

Strategically, we're prioritizing higher-margin growth corridors. We expect alternatives to reach 25% of AUM by year-end 2025 through targeted hires in infrastructure debt and evergreen structures, capitalizing on the $1.5 trillion global dry powder in privates. In equities, we're leaning into active alpha in small/mid-cap and emerging markets, where our 3-year information ratios outperform benchmarks by 0.4, justifying 10-20 bps premia over passives. Looking ahead, we guide to full-year management fee revenue of $5.0-$5.2 billion, implying 8-10% growth, with average fee rates stabilizing at 44-45 bps as mix shifts dominate. This positions us well in an industry where fee pressure is structural but navigable through product innovation and client-centric tech.

Turning now to trends in our operating margin, which continue to reflect the resilience of our franchise amid a dynamic macroeconomic backdrop. Operating margin—defined as adjusted operating income divided by net revenues—remains a key barometer of our operational efficiency in the asset management industry. It captures our ability to scale AUM profitably while navigating fee compression, product mix shifts, and escalating investments in technology and compliance.

For the quarter, we delivered an operating margin of 38.2%, up 210 basis points year-over-year from 36.1% in Q2 2023, and sequentially flat from 38.1% in Q1 2024. This marks our sixth consecutive quarter of margin expansion, bringing our trailing twelve-month margin to a robust 37.5%—well above the industry peer average of around 32% as reported in recent earnings from firms like T. Rowe Price and Franklin Templeton. On a full-year basis, we now expect FY2024 margins to land at 37-38%, versus our prior guide of 36-37%, driven by stronger-than-expected AUM net inflows and disciplined expense management.

On the revenue side, our net revenues grew 11% year-over-year, fueled by average AUM of $1.52 trillion—wait, average AUM of $570 billion, up 12% YoY, benefiting from equity market tailwinds—the S&P 500 up 18% YTD—and $28 billion in organic net inflows, primarily into our active fixed income and alternatives strategies. However, average management fees dipped 3 basis points to 44 bps, reflecting ongoing industry-wide fee compression, particularly in our beta ETF suite, where fees averaged just 12 bps, comparable to BlackRock's iShares core offerings. Institutional mandates, which comprise 62% of AUM, held steady at 38 bps, while retail channels saw slightly more pressure at 52 bps due to competitive pricing in wealth management platforms like Schwab and Fidelity.

Expense leverage was the real margin story: Adjusted operating expenses rose only 6% YoY to $1.11 billion, or 61.7% of revenues—down 280 bps from 64.5% last year. Compensation and benefits, our largest line at 42% of opex, increased 5% but declined as a percentage of revenue to 25.2%, thanks to performance-based variable pay aligning with our 8% ROE target. Non-comp expenses, including G&A and distribution, grew 7% but benefited from scale, with tech and data investments now representing 15% of opex, up from 12% two years ago.

Regionally, performance varied meaningfully: North America, 72% of AUM, margins here expanded to 41%, supported by strong retail inflows into our ESG equity funds—$12 billion YTD—and lower distribution costs via direct indexing platforms. US institutional clients, including defined contribution plans, favored our active quant strategies amid volatility. EMEA, 18% of AUM, margins compressed slightly to 32% due to MiFID II unbundling pressures, which shaved 2 bps off fees in equity mandates. However, alternatives like private credit saw 15% AUM growth, with fees holding at 85 bps. Asia-Pacific, 10% of AUM, our brightest spot, with margins at 35% on 22% AUM growth from sovereign wealth fund mandates in China and Japan. Local currency bond ETFs captured $5 billion in flows, offsetting yen weakness.

Product mix shifts amplified these trends. Actives, at 55% of AUM, delivered 52% of revenues with 65 bps fees, while passives/ETFs, 35% of AUM, contributed 25% of revenues at 18 bps but grew AUM 20% YoY, mimicking Vanguard's low-cost dominance. Alternatives and multi-asset solutions, 10% of AUM, punched above their weight with 23% margins contribution at 110 bps fees, underscoring our push into private markets amid the $10 trillion illiquids opportunity, as highlighted in Preqin data.

Technical initiatives have been pivotal to this efficiency. We've accelerated our Digital Alpha platform, an AI/ML-driven suite for portfolio construction and risk analytics, which reduced middle- and back-office costs by 18% in model pilots. Automation via RPA has cut trade settlement times by 40%, aligning with DTCC's T+1 push, and our cloud migration to AWS saved $45 million annually in data center expenses. In compliance, regtech investments preempted SEC private fund reforms, limiting fee leakage. These initiatives target a 20% opex reduction per $100 billion AUM over the next three years, positioning us ahead of peers like State Street Global Advisors.

Strategically, we're laser-focused on high-conviction active and alternatives to counter fee decay—aiming for 60% of inflows from 55+ bps products by 2025—while scaling low-cost betas for distribution breadth. M&A remains opportunistic; our recent acquisition of a European quant boutique adds $50 billion AUM at 70 bps blended fees. Risks include persistent inflation eroding real yields in fixed income and geopolitical tensions curbing APAC flows, but our diversified footprint and 15% expense-to-revenue CAGR target provide buffers.

I'd also like to address our compensation ratio, defined as total compensation expense—including base salaries, performance-based bonuses, equity awards, and benefits—expressed as a percentage of net revenue. In asset management, this ratio is a critical barometer of operating leverage, talent productivity, and our ability to scale amid fee compression and the shift toward passive strategies. High-caliber portfolio managers, research analysts, and distribution talent drive alpha generation and AUM flows, so we prioritize competitive pay, but disciplined expense management is equally vital.

For the full year to date in 2024, tracking toward our full-year expectations, our compensation ratio is at 47.2%, a 320 basis point improvement from 50.4% in 2023, and the lowest in our five-year history. In Q2 alone, it was 46.8%, down from 49.5% in the prior-year quarter. This reflects robust revenue growth outpacing our variable comp accrual, driven by a 22% increase in average AUM fueled by $28 billion in net inflows—particularly into our low-cost ETFs and model portfolios—and favorable market tailwinds from the S&P 500's rally.

Breaking this down, base salaries and benefits, largely fixed, represented about 22% of total comp expense, flat year-over-year as we held headcount steady at 2,450 full-time equivalents. The real leverage came from variable pay: annual bonuses and long-term incentive plans totaled $420 million year-to-date, or 36% of comp, down 150 bps as a percentage of revenue due to our outperformance-based structure. Over 70% of bonuses are tied to risk-adjusted returns above benchmarks like the MSCI World Index, client net flows, and ESG integration metrics, aligning pay with shareholder value. Our LTIPs, heavily weighted toward performance-vested RSUs linked to three-year TSR versus peers like T. Rowe Price and Franklin Templeton, vested at 115% of target for the recent cycle.

Regionally, we saw some variance: In the Americas, generating 62% of revenue, the ratio was 48.1%—higher due to elevated talent costs in New York and San Francisco amid competition for quant researchers from firms like Renaissance Technologies. EMEA came in leaner at 44.5%, benefiting from our London and Luxembourg hubs where regulatory tailwinds for UCITS funds drove 15% AUM growth with modest headcount adds. APAC was our efficiency standout at 42.3%, thanks to offshoring back-office functions to Singapore and leveraging our joint venture with a major Japanese keiretsu for distribution without proportional comp inflation.

Key trends include revenue diversification: Active equity and fixed income fees, while facing 5-10 bps compression from Vanguard-style passives, were offset by 30% growth in our alternatives platform—private credit and infrastructure funds—yielding 45-60 bps. This scaled revenue without linear headcount growth. Technology investments: We've deployed $150 million over two years in AI-driven tools, including natural language processing for sentiment analysis in our Global Equity strategy and machine learning for portfolio optimization in our Core Bond ETF. This has boosted analyst productivity by 25%, allowing us to maintain alpha—our active funds beat benchmarks by 210 bps net of fees—with 10% fewer research staff than in 2023.

Looking ahead, we're targeting a 46-48% compensation ratio for full-year 2024, assuming AUM growth to $580-600 billion on 8-12% organic inflows and mid-single-digit market appreciation. This guidance incorporates a 5% base salary increase for retention—critical in a war for ESG and quant talent—but moderated by capping bonuses at 110% of target unless we exceed 15% revenue growth. Strategically, we're accelerating 'talent arbitrage': Expanding our Bengaluru tech center for alpha research, which handles 40% of our systematic strategies at 30% lower cost than U.S. equivalents, and piloting variable comp deferrals into client-aligned deferred units. Amid rising rates and potential U.S. election volatility, we'll prioritize hires in multi-asset solutions and derivatives trading desks to capture volatility premia. Our sub-48% ratio demonstrates the scalability of our franchise—much like BlackRock's model but with our active edge—positioning us for EPS expansion even in a fee-pressured world.

Michael Reynolds: Thank you, Emily. On the investment front, we continue to focus on delivering strong risk-adjusted returns for our clients. Our key strategies performed well, particularly in equities and alternatives. We are navigating the current market environment by leveraging our proprietary research and quant tools. We launched GAP Private Credit Opportunities this quarter, and the early reception has been positive, with $4.5 billion in commitments already.

Today, I'd like to dive deep into our fund performance relative to peers and benchmarks—a core pillar of our value proposition in an increasingly competitive landscape dominated by fee compression and the shift toward passive strategies. Our disciplined, active management approach continues to deliver compelling results, generating alpha through proprietary research, factor-based tilts, and opportunistic positioning. Over the trailing 12 months ended June 30, 2024, our core strategies outperformed their benchmarks by an average of 210 basis points, or bps, net of fees, while ranking in the top quartile against a peer universe of over 500 funds per Morningstar Direct data. This marks our 10th consecutive quarter of median outperformance across our flagship products, underscoring the efficacy of our bottom-up stock selection and macro overlays.

Let's break this down by asset class, starting with equities, which represent 55% of our AUM. In U.S. large-cap growth, our Global Growth Equity Fund returned 28.4% over the past 12 months, surpassing the S&P 500 Growth Index by 450 bps and beating 87% of peers in the Morningstar Large Growth category, including heavyweights like Fidelity Contrafund and T. Rowe Price Blue Chip Growth. This edge came from our overweight in secular growers like NVIDIA and Broadcom—beneficiaries of the AI infrastructure boom—while underweighting cyclicals exposed to softening consumer spending. Our Sharpe ratio of 1.65 handily exceeded the benchmark's 1.22, reflecting superior risk-adjusted returns amid elevated volatility from Fed tightening.

Shifting to U.S. large-cap value, the Global Value Opportunities Fund delivered 22.1%, outpacing the Russell 1000 Value Index by 320 bps and top-decile peers like Dodge & Cox Stock. Here, our forensic credit analysis on financials and energy names paid off; we rotated early into regional banks post-SVB stress, capturing a 15% rebound in that subsector.

Internationally, our Global Equity Fund returned 18.7%, edging the MSCI ACWI ex-U.S. by 280 bps and ranking top-quartile versus BlackRock's iShares MSCI ACWI ETF and peers like American Funds New World. Europe lagged at +12% due to persistent energy headwinds from the Ukraine conflict, where we maintained a defensive underweight in German industrials. In contrast, our overweight in Japan—via positions in Sony and Tokyo Electron—added 150 bps of alpha, fueled by Abenomics 2.0 wage inflation and yen depreciation tailwinds. Emerging markets were a standout: our EM Alpha Fund surged 26.2%, beating the MSCI EM Index by 410 bps and 92% of peers like Templeton EM. India and Mexico drove this, with tactical calls on IT services—Infosys up 35%—and nearshoring plays, offsetting China underperformance from regulatory overhang.

On fixed income, comprising 25% of AUM, we navigated a brutal rate-hike environment with agility. The Global Core Bond Fund posted a 12-month total return of 2.8%, outperforming the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index's -1.2% by 400 bps and top-quintile peers like PIMCO Total Return and Vanguard Total Bond Market. Duration management was key: we shortened to 4.2 years versus the benchmark's 6.1, while layering in high-conviction corporate credit—AAA to BBB spreads tightened 25 bps in Q2 alone. Our structured credit sleeve, including CLOs and ABS, yielded 5.2% YTD, capturing illiquidity premia without excessive tracking error of just 1.8%.

In high-yield, the Global HY Income Fund returned 9.6%, topping the ICE BofA HY Index by 150 bps and 78% of Lipper peers. We avoided the energy covenant resets that plagued some competitors, focusing on U.S. consumer cyclicals with EBITDA cushions above 3x.

Alternatives and multi-asset strategies, at 20% of AUM, shone brightest. Our flagship Absolute Return Fund generated 11.2% net, with a stellar information ratio of 0.85 versus the HFRI Fund Weighted Composite's 7.8%. Long/short equity and event-driven bets—like our activist stake in a mid-cap tech turnaround—delivered 300 bps of alpha. Private markets AUM grew 18% YoY to $65 billion, with our direct lending vintage funds achieving 14.5% IRR net, outperforming Cambridge Associates medians by 250 bps amid dry powder deployment in sponsor-backed deals.

Technically, we've invested heavily in our next-gen quant platform, launched in Q1 with $50 million in capex. This integrates machine learning for alpha decay detection and dynamic factor rotation—momentum, quality, low vol—across 80% of our equity mandates. Result? Style drift minimized to under 2%, and our quant-enhanced small-cap fund beat the Russell 2000 by 600 bps. We're also scaling ESG integration via our proprietary Sustainability Scorecard, now covering 95% of holdings; our Sustainable Equity Fund returned 24.5%, top-decile in Morningstar's ESG category, attracting $12 billion in inflows from European pensions chasing Article 8 compliance.

Strategic insights: In a world where passive AUM hit 50% market share per EPFR data, our active conviction—average position size 4.5%, highest-conviction 15%—differentiated us. Client retention hit 98%, with organic flows of $18 billion YTD, reversing industry outflows. Fee compression? We've held gross fees at 65 bps on core strategies by bundling beta overlays with alpha mandates, while launching low-cost active ETFs like our Global AI Tech ETF, which has gathered $2.5 billion since inception, tracking a custom NVIDIA/Palantir-heavy index with 50 bps expense ratio.

Looking ahead, we're positioning for Fed rate cuts—probabilistically 75 bps by year-end per our models—by extending duration selectively in mortgages and extending EM credit exposure. Risks? Geopolitical flares in the Middle East could spike oil, but our 5% energy hedge mitigates. Overall, our track record positions us to capture share in a $120 trillion global AUM market growing at 6% CAGR.

David Patel: Thank you, Michael. From a distribution perspective, we saw strong inflows into our active equity and alternatives funds. Our efforts to expand our reach in EMEA and APAC are paying off, as evidenced by $18 billion in long-term net inflows.

Before moving on, I'd like to unpack our net flows in detail, as they remain a key driver of our organic AUM growth and fee-related revenue trajectory. For the quarter, we delivered industry-leading net inflows of $18.2 billion, bringing year-to-date net flows to $52.4 billion—a robust 28% increase over the prior-year period. This marks our 11th straight quarter of positive net flows, with organic growth now accounting for 62% of our total AUM expansion to $585 billion. Excluding market appreciation, these flows underscore the strength of our multi-asset class franchise amid a volatile macro environment.

Breaking this down by key drivers: fund performance, market trends, and our strategic initiatives, with some regional and product-specific color. Performance has been the standout driver this quarter, contributing approximately 45% to our net flow momentum. Our active equity strategies outperformed their benchmarks by an average of 320 basis points over the trailing 12 months, with particular strength in our Global Equity Fund, which returned 22.4% net of fees versus the MSCI World Index's 18.7%. This propelled $9.8 billion in long-term equity inflows, including a $2.5 billion institutional mandate from a major European pension fund attracted by our consistent top-quartile Lipper rankings.

In fixed income, we saw $4.2 billion in net inflows to our short-duration and investment-grade credit sleeves, driven by outperformance amid the Fed's 50bps rate cut in September. The Global Core Bond Fund, for instance, delivered 4.8% YTD versus the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index's 2.1%, benefiting from our tactical overweight in agency MBS and high-quality corporates. Conversely, we experienced modest outflows of $1.1 billion from longer-duration strategies, where redemptions totaled 3% of AUM—largely from tactical retail reallocations as 10-year Treasury yields stabilized around 4.1%.

Alternatives rounded out the picture with $4.7 billion in inflows, led by our private credit and infrastructure funds. Our GAP Private Credit Partners VI vintage closed at $12 billion, exceeding its $10 billion target, thanks to 650bps excess returns over high-yield benchmarks, appealing to yield-hungry insurers and sovereign wealth funds.

Market dynamics amplified performance-driven flows, accounting for another 30% of the quarter's momentum. The ongoing AI and tech rally—S&P 500 up 12% in Q2—drove $6.3 billion into our semi-transparent active ETFs, including the Global Tech Innovators ETF, which captured 15% market share growth in its category, mirroring flows into peers like ARK Innovation or Invesco QQQ. Broader equity beta exposure benefited from retail platforms like Schwab and Fidelity, where our model delivery partnerships saw a 22% uptick in advisor allocations.

On the fixed-income side, the disinflation narrative—CPI cooling to 2.4%—sparked a bond rally, with $3.5 billion flowing into our ESG-labeled funds. Sustainable investing remains a megatrend: our Global Sustainable Global Bond ETF gathered $1.8 billion, up 40% YoY, as EU SFDR regulations and U.S. SEC climate disclosures pushed institutional demand. However, energy sector volatility amid OPEC+ cuts tempered flows into commodity-linked strategies, resulting in flat $200 million net flows there.

Geopolitically, Middle East tensions boosted our gold and defense-themed overlays, adding $900 million, while China's stimulus package drove $1.2 billion into our EM Asia ex-China equity fund, offsetting prior outflows from property-exposed mandates.

Regionally, North America contributed 55% of inflows at $10 billion, fueled by U.S. wirehouse channels like Morgan Stanley and Merrill Lynch where our SMAs grew 15% via performance fee waivers on top-decile funds. EMEA delivered $5.1 billion, with UK DC pensions favoring our lower-beta multi-asset credit solutions amid gilt yield curve steepening. APAC was the star at $3.1 billion—or 17% of total—driven by a $1.4 billion sovereign mandate from Korea and retail growth in Australia via our wrap platform integrations, where fee compression to 45bps on ETFs helped win 12% wallet share.

Institutionals drove 68% of flows, $12.4 billion, reflecting RFP wins from our quant-enhanced active strategies, while retail/intermediary channels added $5.8 billion, bolstered by direct indexing pilots reducing tax drag by 120bps for HNWIs.

Underpinning these flows are targeted initiatives. We launched three active ETFs in Q2—totaling $2.1 billion in seed capital—leveraging our proprietary Aladdin-like risk platform for daily liquidity and sub-20bps expense ratios, directly competing with BlackRock's iShares and State Street's SPDRs. Our robo-advisor arm, Global Digital Portfolios, scaled to $8 billion AUM with AI-driven personalization, capturing 25% millennial inflows via zero-commission trades.

Strategically, we're leaning into 'alternatives democratization' with interval funds targeting retail RIAs, projecting $15-20 billion in FY25 flows. We've also deepened advisor enablement via our Global Insights portal, delivering predictive flow analytics that improved retention by 8%. Amid fee pressure—blended fee rate at 38bps, down 2bps YoY—we're offsetting via scale and active share gains—now 42% of AUM versus Vanguard's passive-heavy mix.

Looking ahead, we expect Q3 net flows of $20-25 billion, supported by year-end rebalancing and our pipeline of $35 billion in institutional RFPs. Performance dispersion in a slowing growth environment should favor our skill-based boutiques, while rate cut cycles sustain fixed-income tailwinds.

Johnathan Hale: In summary, we are confident in our ability to continue delivering value to our shareholders. We are focused on executing our strategic priorities and capitalizing on the opportunities ahead. This includes guiding to full-year management fee revenue of $5.0-$5.2 billion, operating margins of 37-38%, and sustained net inflows driven by our performance edge and product innovation.

Operator: Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Ben Smith with Goldman Sachs.

Ben Smith: Good morning. Can you provide more details on the management fee revenue and average fee rate trends, especially the mix shift impacts?

Johnathan Hale: Thanks, Ben. Emily, do you want to take that?

Emily Carter: Absolutely, Johnathan. As I detailed earlier, our management fee revenue of $1.25 billion benefited from AUM growth via $18 billion inflows and $25 billion market returns, with the blended fee rate at 44.5 bps. The modest compression was offset by alternatives now at 22% of AUM with 85 bps fees, private credit raising $4.5 billion, and ESG UCITS at $45 billion. Regional strength in APAC at 52 bps and our fee optimization engine reduced waivers by 5%. We see stabilization ahead as mix shifts dominate.

Ben Smith: Thank you. And a follow-up on trends in operating margin—how sustainable is the 38.2% with tech investments ramping?

Emily Carter: Great question, Ben. The 210 bps YoY expansion to 38.2% came from revenue growth outpacing 6% opex rise, with comp at 25.2% of revenue and tech at 15% of opex. Digital Alpha cut costs 18%, RPA sped settlements 40%, and AWS saved $45 million. Regionally, North America at 41%, APAC at 35%. We target 20% opex reduction per $100B AUM, guiding 37-38% for the year.

Operator: Our next question comes from Lisa Chen with Morningstar.

Lisa Chen: Good morning. Could you elaborate on the performance of the Global Equity Fund?

Michael Reynolds: Morning, Lisa. Our Global Equity Fund returned 18.7% over 12 months, +280 bps over MSCI ACWI ex-U.S., top-quartile vs. peers. Japan overweight added 150 bps via Sony and Tokyo Electron, EM Alpha at 26.2% beat MSCI EM by 410 bps on India/Mexico calls. Quant platform minimizes drift under 2%, Sharpe superior across the board.

Lisa Chen: And how is the new product, GAP Private Credit Opportunities, performing relative to expectations?

David Patel: Thanks, Lisa. Early reception exceeds expectations with $4.5 billion commitments at 1.25% fee +15% carry. It's driving alts inflows, part of $4.7 billion quarterly, with vintage IRRs outperforming benchmarks. Institutional demand strong from pensions, aligning with our alternatives push to 25% AUM by 2025.

Operator: Thank you. There are no further questions at this time. I'd like to turn the call back over to Johnathan for closing remarks.

Johnathan Hale: Thank you for joining us today. We appreciate your interest in Global Asset Partners. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
